Senses.Explanation: “Each of you, trust that your own mind is Buddha” is Mazu’s instruction to every person in the assembly. His next sentence identifies this mind as Buddha-mind; when a monk later asks why he says mind itself is Buddha, Mazu answers that it is to stop a small child’s crying.

Senses.PreferredTarget: each goes onward on their own course
AlternateTargets: each goes on along their own road
each hurries onward on their own way
Senses.Explanation: “Each goes on along their own road” completes the line “meeting without dismounting,” depicting an encounter that does not interrupt either traveler. Dajue Huailian pairs it with meeting without dismounting; Wuqu Rukong only preserves and quotes that exchange. Wanru Tongwei quotes Zhenjing’s seasonal verse, then objects that it makes people hurry too much and answers with an already-present matter requiring no journey. Muyun Tongmen has a layman use the line to dismiss him to his quarters, but physically catches a monk and says another cannot lead one by the hand. Tian’an Sheng uses the full line to close a contrast between much speaking and little speaking.
Senses.Note: The “course ahead” is the road each party continues after an encounter, not a career. Its fixed companion line is “meeting without dismounting.”

Senses.PreferredTarget: If the tiger is not real, burying an arrow to its feathers is wasted effort

Senses.Note: The image recalls an arrow driven deep into something mistaken for a tiger. It warns that force and skill cannot make a false target real. In these records a master may use it to reject a student’s reply or to question whether an old case has actually reached its mark.

Senses.Explanation: If the tiger is not real, burying an arrow to its feathers is wasted effort questions a forceful answer aimed at the wrong thing. Guxue uses the line while judging an old case about finding a thief. Yunwai replies with it to a student who offers a polished verse. Linwo gives it as a direct answer when a monk asks for instruction at a teaching assembly. Dachuan ends a short sermon with it after opposing “is” and “is not.” Shitian says it after describing his own demanding gate. Pingshi uses it after asking whether a quick claim of understanding can be accepted.

Senses.Explanation: A person who mistakes reflected brightness for the matter itself is ‘playing with light and shadows.’ The witnesses apply the rebuke to moon imagery, clever answers, and a practitioner still occupied with the brightness of present awareness. The phrase appears in Feiyin Tongrong’s Recorded Sayings, in Juelang Daosheng’s Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie, and in Ruibai Mingxue’s Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Rujiu Ruibai.

Senses.Explanation: The term is attested as a stock Chan rebuke. Baishan Dekai applies it in sequence to talking of the lineage and teachings, of Chan and the Way, and of mind and nature. Yuanwu applies it to people who misread Bodhidharma's 'vast, no holy' and to Xianglin's offering words that displayed his understanding; another collection calls such people 'fellows who play with the vital spirit.' A record also applies the phrase to people sitting woodenly and guarding a dead corpse. The targets vary—speech, presented understanding, or fixed conduct—but the phrase remains the same disparaging action. The sampled records leave the literal 'vital spirit' unglossed.

Senses.Note: “A fellow playing empty tricks” is a sharp verdict on a response that presents confidence without meeting the question. Miyun says it after a layman praises his constant teaching. Shiqi says it after a monk’s shout leaves him without another word; Sanyi after a monk copies a raised fist. Dabian rejects a borrowed place-name answer, Shiguan checks a dramatic exit, and Dabo says it when a grand line collapses into silence. In each case the teacher tests what the person can do next.
